title: Client and server: what lives where
story:
The work of an application gets divided between a machine the user controls and one you control, and the division is not a matter of taste. Two facts decide almost all of it.

The first is trust. Anything running on the user's machine is running on hardware you do not control, in a runtime they can inspect, modify or replace. Every check performed there is a suggestion. This is why validation in the browser and validation on the server are not duplicated effort, despite looking like the same code written twice — they are different features. The client-side check exists to tell a well-intentioned user immediately that a date is malformed, which is a usability property. The server-side check exists because a hostile user will not run your client at all; they will send the request directly. Remove the first and the application becomes annoying. Remove the second and it becomes undefended.

The second is the cost of the boundary itself. The protocol is defined as a stateless application-level protocol, and its specification defines the architecture and terminology shared by all versions — statelessness being a property of the protocol rather than of any application built on it, which is worth separating because applications plainly do have state. What matters for placement is that crossing the boundary is charged per exchange, and the resource it consumes is the one that improves least: bandwidth improves much more quickly than latency across disks, networks, memories and processors, with bandwidth improving by more than the square of the improvement in latency. So a design that adds a round trip is spending the resource that is not getting cheaper, and a design that fetches more in one exchange is spending the one that is.

Which gives a usable rule. Things that must be authoritative, durable or trusted go on the server: the record of what happened, the decisions that have consequences, the secrets. Things that make the interaction feel immediate go on the client: rendering, transient interface state, optimistic feedback. And when in doubt about a chatty interaction, prefer one larger exchange over several small ones, because the cost you are avoiding is per crossing.

The failure mode worth naming is not putting things in the wrong place — it is putting the same thing in both places and letting them disagree. Two copies of a rule about what constitutes a valid order will drift, and when they do the one on the server wins silently, producing rejections that the client believed were impossible. If a rule must exist in both, derive both from one definition rather than maintaining two.

problem.name: Placement across a trust boundary
problem.shape: An application's work must be divided between a machine you control and one you do not, separated by a link charged per exchange.
tell: a rule exists in the interface code and nowhere else
a screen makes several sequential requests before it can render
the same business rule is written twice in two languages
state is being kept on the server for a user between requests
problem.move: Place work by what it requires: authority, durability and secrets on the server, responsiveness on the client. Treat every crossing as the expensive operation it is and prefer fewer larger exchanges. Where a rule must appear on both sides, generate both from a single definition rather than maintaining two.
problem.invariant: Anything on the client runs on hardware you do not control, so every client-side check is advisory and must be repeated where it can be enforced.
problem.breaks: Duplication is the correct answer for security and the wrong answer for maintenance, and the two pull against each other. Two hand-maintained copies of a rule will drift, and when they do the authoritative side rejects requests the advisory side promised would succeed — so the safe design is not one copy but one definition with two derived enforcements.

cost.time: a round trip per crossing, spending the resource that improves least
cost.space: work placed on the client ships to every user, so logic there costs download size and start-up time
cost.beats: putting everything on the server, which is trustworthy and unresponsive, and putting everything on the client, which is responsive and undefended

worked.problem: Why does validation performed in the browser have to be performed again on the server?
worked.reasoning:
Because they are not the same feature, despite being the same rule — and only one of them is enforcement.

Anything running on the user's machine runs on hardware you do not control, in a runtime they can open, modify or bypass entirely. A hostile user does not run your client; they send the request directly, with whatever contents they choose. So a check performed there is a statement about what your interface does, not a constraint on what your server will accept.

The server-side check is therefore the only one that is enforcement. It sits on the machine you control, on the path every request must actually take, and no client behaviour can route around it. That is the security boundary, and it is singular.

Which raises the fair question of why keep the client-side one at all — and the answer is that it does a genuinely different job. It tells a well-intentioned user immediately that a date is malformed or a field is empty, without a round trip and without losing what they typed. That is a usability property and it is worth having. Remove it and the application becomes slow and irritating; remove the server-side one and the application becomes undefended. Different removals, different failures.

So the duplication is correct. What I would flag is the trap it creates, because this is where it actually goes wrong in practice. Two hand-maintained copies of a rule about what constitutes valid input will drift — someone relaxes a limit on one side, tightens a format on the other — and when they drift the authoritative side wins silently. The result is rejections the interface believed were impossible, which are hard to diagnose because the client's model of the rules is not the enforced one.

The handling is to keep one definition and derive both enforcements from it: a shared schema, a generated validator, a single source the two sides are built from. That preserves the security property, which requires two enforcement points, while removing the maintenance property that causes the drift.

And I would extend the principle beyond validation, since it generalises: anything the client computes that has consequences — a price, an entitlement, a permission — is advisory in exactly the same way and must be recomputed where it can be trusted.

problem.practice: Take one rule your interface enforces and check whether the server enforces it too. Then send the request directly, bypassing the interface, with a value the interface would have refused. Whatever happens next is your actual security posture.

beats.broke: An application's work must be divided between a machine the user controls and one you control, separated by a link whose cost is paid per exchange rather than per byte.
beats.fix: Place each piece by what it needs — trust and durable data on your side, responsiveness and interaction on theirs — and treat every crossing of the boundary as the expensive operation it is.
beats.cost: Anything on the client runs on hardware you cannot trust, so every client-side check has to be repeated on the server, and that duplication is not waste but the security model.

interview.q: Why does validation performed in the browser have to be performed again on the server?
interview.trap: Treating it as defensive redundancy in case the client fails. The client cannot fail in the relevant sense because a hostile user never runs it — and the real trap is the two copies drifting, which is solved by one definition with two derived enforcements rather than by one copy.
